questions.question: Which patterns make a Python API client reliable in production?
questions.title: Production-Ready Python API Client Patterns
questions.direct_answer: A reliable API client has an owned Session, explicit timeouts, status and schema validation, bounded safe retries, pagination and rate-limit handling, secret redaction, and useful observability. These are one coherent client policy, not independent patches added after failures occur.

interviewer_intent.testing: How ownership, reliability policy, validation, pagination, and observability form one API-client boundary.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Scattering direct Requests calls with different timeouts and error behavior throughout business code.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Return domain-friendly values or typed client errors while keeping protocol policy centralized.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Centralize base URL, Session ownership, headers, auth, and error translation.
Set connect/read timeouts and retry only transient, repeatable operations.
Handle pagination and 429/Retry-After as normal protocol behavior.
Validate decoded data before business code uses it.
Record latency, status, attempts, and request IDs while redacting secrets.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A production API client should be a small boundary around the remote service rather than scattered requests.get() calls. I give it an owned Session for connection reuse and shared headers, a base URL, authentication, explicit connect and read timeouts, and a clear method for each remote operation.

Every method classifies results in the same order: transport, HTTP status, representation decoding, and application validation. For example, list_orders() may follow cursor pages, accept 200 JSON, turn 401 into an authentication error, honor 429 Retry-After, and reject a supposedly successful payload whose items field is not a list.

Retries are bounded and limited to transient failures when the request is safely repeatable. I use backoff and jitter, respect server rate-limit guidance, and keep all attempts inside the caller's latency budget. A POST is retried only when the endpoint provides an idempotency contract or the operation is otherwise known to be repeatable.

The client also makes operations observable. Metrics capture latency, status groups, retry count, and failure category. Logs include an operation name and server request ID, while Authorization, cookies, personal data, and large bodies are redacted. Tests use deterministic fake responses for success, each failure layer, pagination termination, and retry limits.

The boundary stays narrow: it returns domain-friendly values or typed client errors, not raw response objects throughout the application. Together these patterns make behavior consistent under both normal traffic and partial failure without hiding HTTP semantics.

sections.title: Reliability as a complete client workflow
sections.content:
Reliability starts with ownership. One service-client object owns transport state and policy; individual methods describe endpoint semantics. This prevents different call sites from choosing conflicting timeouts, retry lists, or authentication headers.

The request path includes capacity decisions as well as correctness. Pagination caps memory use, streaming avoids loading large bodies at once, rate-limit handling protects both sides, and concurrency limits stop a local workload from overwhelming an upstream service.

The failure model should be small and stable for callers. AuthenticationFailure, NotFound, RateLimited, TransientUpstream, InvalidResponse, and similar categories can retain status and original causes without forcing business code to understand every Requests exception.

Testing should control time and responses. Fake adapters or a local test server can prove retry counts, backoff decisions, cursor changes, timeout translation, and redaction. Live upstream calls belong in a smaller integration suite because they are slower and less deterministic.

sections.title: One client boundary owns the HTTP policy
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Application use case] --> C[Service client methods]
  C --> P[Policy: auth, timeout, retry, pagination]
  P --> S[Session and connection pool]
  S --> U[Upstream API]
  U --> V[Status, decode, validate]
  V --> C
  C --> O[Domain value or typed client error]
  C -. metrics and redacted logs .-> M[Observability]
```

questions.question: How should a Python client consume a paginated API?
questions.title: Consuming Paginated APIs Safely
questions.direct_answer: A paginated client should process one page at a time, read the server's next-page signal, stop on an explicit end condition, and guard against repeated cursors. It should preserve ordering and deduplication rules defined by the API instead of guessing from page size alone.

interviewer_intent.testing: Cursor, offset, and link pagination with correct continuation and termination rules.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Stopping only because a page is short or reusing a repeated cursor forever.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain data-change consistency separately from pagination mechanics.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Follow the API's documented next link, cursor, or page metadata.
Stop when the explicit continuation value is absent, not only when a page is short.
Process or yield items page by page to keep memory bounded.
Detect a repeated cursor so a server bug cannot create an infinite loop.
Expect data to change between pages unless the API promises a stable snapshot.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A paginated API splits a collection into responses and provides a rule for reaching the next one. The client should follow that documented rule—such as a next URL, opaque cursor, or page number—rather than inventing an end condition from the number of returned items.

For example, a cursor response may contain items and next_cursor. I request the first page without a cursor, yield or process its items, and pass the returned cursor to the next call. When next_cursor is null, the traversal is complete. I keep a set of seen cursors so a repeated token becomes a clear error instead of an infinite loop.

Cursor pagination is usually better for a changing large collection because it gives the server a continuation position, while offset pagination is simple but can skip or duplicate records when rows are inserted or deleted between calls. Neither model automatically gives a stable snapshot; that guarantee must come from the API contract.

Each page still needs a timeout, status handling, rate-limit handling, and schema validation. Processing pages incrementally limits memory and allows progress, while materializing every item may be appropriate only when the collection is known to be small. The safe pattern is server-directed continuation with an explicit stop condition and consistency assumptions.

sections.title: Pagination state and termination rules
sections.content:
Pagination is a protocol between client and server. Offset/page-number protocols expose a position the client can calculate. Cursor protocols give the client an opaque continuation token that must be returned unchanged. Link-based protocols provide the next target directly.

Termination and consistency are independent. A missing next token ends traversal, but it does not prove that the collection stayed unchanged while pages were fetched. APIs may offer snapshot tokens, stable sort keys, or event streams when exact consistency matters.

Streaming one page at a time creates natural backpressure. A generator can hand items to the caller without storing the entire collection. The implementation still needs a maximum-page or repeated-token guard for malformed upstream behavior.

sections.title: Cursor pagination loop
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Request page with current cursor] --> B[Validate items and next_cursor]
  B --> C[Yield/process items]
  C --> D{next_cursor present?}
  D -->|no| E[Complete]
  D -->|yes| F{Cursor seen before?}
  F -->|yes| G[Stop with protocol error]
  F -->|no| A
```

sections.title: Worked Python example
sections.content:
```python
from collections.abc import Iterator
import requests

def iter_items(session: requests.Session, url: str) -> Iterator[dict]:
    cursor = None
    seen: set[str] = set()
    while True:
        response = session.get(url, params={"cursor": cursor} if cursor else {}, timeout=8)
        response.raise_for_status()
        data = response.json()
        items = data.get("items") if isinstance(data, dict) else None
        if not isinstance(items, list):
            raise ValueError("page must contain an items list")
        yield from items
        cursor = data.get("next_cursor")
        if cursor is None:
            return
        if not isinstance(cursor, str) or cursor in seen:
            raise ValueError("invalid or repeated pagination cursor")
        seen.add(cursor)
```

questions.question: How should a Python API client handle HTTP 429 rate limits and Retry-After?
questions.title: Handling HTTP 429 and Retry-After
questions.direct_answer: Treat 429 as a request-rate signal, read Retry-After when present, wait only within the caller's deadline, and retry with a strict limit when the operation is safe. Add jitter and local concurrency or rate limits so the client reduces pressure instead of repeatedly colliding with the server limit.

interviewer_intent.testing: 429 meaning, Retry-After formats, retry budgets, and proactive rate control.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Immediately retrying 429 in a tight loop and creating a synchronized retry storm.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Combine bounded recovery with concurrency limits, caching, batching, and rate-limit metrics.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: 429 means the client has sent too many requests under the server's policy.
Retry-After may be delay-seconds or an HTTP date.
Respect the delay only when time and retry budgets permit.
Use jitter and bounded attempts; never loop forever on 429.
Prevent repeated 429s with client-side rate or concurrency control.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
HTTP 429 means the server is rate-limiting the client. I treat it as normal protocol feedback, not as permission to retry immediately. If the response includes Retry-After, its value is either a number of seconds or an HTTP date, and the client can use that as the earliest sensible follow-up time.

For example, Retry-After: 3 asks the client to wait three seconds. I first check whether the operation is safely repeatable and whether three seconds fits the caller's remaining deadline. If so, I wait with a bounded retry count; if not, I return a rate-limited error so the caller can defer the work or respond appropriately.

When no usable header is present, exponential backoff with jitter avoids many workers retrying in lockstep. I also read any API-specific rate-limit headers only according to that API's documentation, because names and units are not universal HTTP rules.

Retries alone are reactive. A production client should limit local concurrency or request rate, cache suitable reads, batch work when supported, and observe 429 counts. It must not hold a web request open indefinitely just to exhaust a retry policy. The goal is cooperative load reduction within a clear time and attempt budget.

sections.title: Rate-limit recovery without duplicate work
sections.content:
Rate limiting protects a shared service by controlling demand over some identity and window. The identity might be an API key, user, IP address, or account. The client cannot infer that policy from status 429 alone, so vendor documentation remains part of the contract.

Retry-After is standardized and can contain delay-seconds or a date. Date parsing must consider clock differences, and any negative result should be treated carefully. A local retry policy should choose a delay that respects the server while remaining inside the operation's deadline.

The best mitigation happens before rejection. A semaphore bounds concurrent calls; a token bucket can pace requests; caches avoid repeat reads; queues smooth bursts. Metrics reveal whether demand permanently exceeds the purchased or documented quota, which requires capacity or product decisions rather than more retries.

sections.title: 429 recovery without a retry storm
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Receive 429] --> B[Read Retry-After if present]
  B --> C{Safe retry and budget remain?}
  C -->|no| D[Return rate-limited result]
  C -->|yes| E[Wait: server delay or backoff + jitter]
  E --> F[Retry once]
  F --> G[Adjust local rate/concurrency]
```
